title: Brain
junior: Your brain is the control centre of your body. It is protected by your skull and three soft wrappings. Different parts do different jobs: thinking and remembering, balance, and keeping your heart and breathing going without you even thinking about it.
definition: The brain is the central information-processing organ of the body and acts as the 'command and control system'; together with the spinal cord it forms the central nervous system (CNS).
structure: Protected by the skull and three cranial meninges: outer dura mater, very thin middle arachnoid and inner pia mater (in contact with brain tissue).
Forebrain: cerebrum, thalamus and hypothalamus.
Midbrain: between the thalamus/hypothalamus and the pons; the cerebral aqueduct passes through it; dorsal corpora quadrigemina.
Hindbrain: pons, cerebellum and medulla oblongata.
Brain stem = midbrain + pons + medulla oblongata.
functions: Controls voluntary movements, balance of the body and the functioning of vital involuntary organs (lungs, heart, kidneys).
Thermoregulation, hunger and thirst, circadian rhythms, endocrine activity (hypothalamus).
Processing of vision, hearing, speech, memory, intelligence, emotions and thoughts.
neetPoints: The limbic system (inner parts of cerebral hemispheres with amygdala and hippocampus) and the hypothalamus regulate sexual behaviour, emotional reactions (excitement, pleasure, rage, fear) and motivation.
Brain stem forms the connection between the brain and the spinal cord.
commonMistakes: The pia mater is the innermost meninx (touching the brain); the dura mater is outermost.

mcqs.stem: The correct order of cranial meninges from outside to inside is:
mcqs.explanation: Outer dura mater, middle arachnoid, inner pia mater.

mcqs.stem: The brain stem consists of:
mcqs.explanation: Midbrain, pons and medulla oblongata form the brain stem.

mcqs.stem: Which part of the brain is involved in the regulation of emotional reactions such as rage and fear, along with the hypothalamus?
mcqs.explanation: The limbic system with the hypothalamus regulates emotions, sexual behaviour and motivation.

title: Cerebrum (cerebral hemispheres)
junior: The cerebrum is the biggest, wrinkly part of your brain. It is split into a left and a right half. It's where you think, learn, remember, see, hear and decide to move.
definition: The cerebrum forms the major part of the human brain; a deep cleft divides it longitudinally into left and right cerebral hemispheres, connected by the corpus callosum.
structure: Cerebral cortex: outer layer of grey matter (neuron cell bodies), thrown into prominent folds.
Inner white matter: myelinated fibre tracts with an opaque white appearance.
Cortex contains motor areas, sensory areas and large association areas.
functions: Association areas are responsible for complex functions like intersensory associations, memory and communication.
Motor areas control voluntary movements; sensory areas receive sensations.
neetPoints: Association areas are neither clearly sensory nor motor in function.
The cerebrum wraps around the thalamus.
commonMistakes: Grey matter is outside (cortex) in the cerebrum but inside in the spinal cord.

mcqs.stem: The two cerebral hemispheres are connected by the:
mcqs.explanation: The corpus callosum is a tract of nerve fibres connecting the hemispheres.

mcqs.stem: Association areas of the cerebral cortex are responsible for:
mcqs.explanation: NCERT: association areas handle complex functions like intersensory associations, memory and communication.

title: Corpus callosum
junior: The corpus callosum is a thick bridge of nerve fibres that lets the left and right halves of your brain talk to each other.
definition: The corpus callosum is a broad tract of myelinated nerve fibres connecting the left and right cerebral hemispheres.
structure: White matter lying at the bottom of the longitudinal fissure.
Forms the roof of the lateral ventricles.
functions: Transfers information between the two hemispheres.
neetPoints: It is the largest commissure (white matter tract) of the brain.

mcqs.stem: The corpus callosum is made of:
mcqs.explanation: It is a tract of nerve fibres — white matter.

mcqs.stem: The corpus callosum is part of the:
mcqs.explanation: It connects the cerebral hemispheres of the forebrain.

title: Thalamus
junior: The thalamus is like a post office in the middle of your brain. Messages from your senses stop here and get sent on to the right place.
definition: The thalamus is a paired forebrain structure around which the cerebrum wraps; it is a major coordinating centre for sensory and motor signalling.
structure: Egg-shaped masses of grey matter on each side of the third ventricle.
functions: Relays and coordinates sensory and motor signals to and from the cerebral cortex.
neetPoints: The hypothalamus lies at the base of the thalamus.

mcqs.stem: The major coordinating centre for sensory and motor signalling is the:
mcqs.explanation: NCERT: the thalamus is a major coordinating centre for sensory and motor signalling.

mcqs.stem: The thalamus is a part of the:
mcqs.explanation: Forebrain = cerebrum, thalamus and hypothalamus.

title: Hypothalamus
junior: The hypothalamus is tiny but very important. It is your body's thermostat, tells you when you're hungry or thirsty, and bosses the pituitary gland around.
definition: The hypothalamus lies at the base of the thalamus; it contains centres that control body temperature and the urge for eating and drinking, and neurosecretory cells that secrete hypothalamic hormones.
structure: Connected to the pituitary by the infundibulum (stalk).
Contains groups of neurosecretory cells (nuclei).
functions: Thermoregulation, hunger, thirst.
Releasing hormones (e.g. GnRH) stimulate, and inhibiting hormones (e.g. somatostatin) inhibit, pituitary secretion; they reach the anterior pituitary through a portal circulatory system.
Synthesises oxytocin and vasopressin, which are transported axonally to the posterior pituitary.
neetPoints: The hypothalamus is the basal part of the diencephalon and regulates a wide spectrum of body functions.
Posterior pituitary is under direct neural regulation of the hypothalamus.

mcqs.stem: Oxytocin and vasopressin are synthesised in the:
mcqs.explanation: They are made by hypothalamic neurosecretory cells and only stored/released by the posterior pituitary.

mcqs.stem: Somatostatin from the hypothalamus:
mcqs.explanation: Somatostatin is an inhibiting hormone that inhibits the release of GH from the pituitary.

title: Midbrain
junior: The midbrain is a short section between the top and bottom parts of your brain. It helps with seeing and hearing reflexes, like turning your head towards a loud bang.
definition: The midbrain is located between the thalamus/hypothalamus of the forebrain and the pons of the hindbrain.
structure: A canal called the cerebral aqueduct passes through it.
Dorsal portion has four round swellings (lobes) called corpora quadrigemina.
Cerebral peduncles on the ventral side.
functions: Visual and auditory reflexes (corpora quadrigemina).
Pathway between forebrain and hindbrain.
neetPoints: Midbrain and hindbrain form the brain stem.

mcqs.stem: Corpora quadrigemina are present in the:
mcqs.explanation: The dorsal midbrain has four round swellings called corpora quadrigemina.

mcqs.stem: The cerebral aqueduct passes through the:
mcqs.explanation: It connects the third and fourth ventricles through the midbrain.

title: Pons
junior: The pons is a bridge in your brain stem that links different parts of the brain. It also helps set how fast you breathe.
definition: The pons is part of the hindbrain consisting of fibre tracts that interconnect different regions of the brain.
structure: Lies in front of the cerebellum, between the midbrain and the medulla.
functions: Relays signals between cerebrum and cerebellum.
Pneumotaxic centre moderates the respiratory rhythm centre.
neetPoints: The pneumotaxic centre in the pons can reduce the duration of inspiration and thereby alter the respiratory rate.

mcqs.stem: The pneumotaxic centre is located in the:
mcqs.explanation: NCERT: a pneumotaxic centre in the pons region moderates the respiratory rhythm centre.

mcqs.stem: The pons mainly consists of:
mcqs.explanation: NCERT: pons consists of fibre tracts that interconnect different regions of the brain.

title: Medulla oblongata
junior: The medulla is at the bottom of your brain, joined to your spinal cord. It runs things you never think about: breathing, heartbeat, swallowing and even sneezing.
definition: The medulla (oblongata) is the lowest part of the brain stem, connected to the spinal cord; it contains centres that control respiration, cardiovascular reflexes and gastric secretions.
structure: Continuous below with the spinal cord at the foramen magnum.
Contains the respiratory rhythm centre and a chemosensitive area.
functions: Respiratory rhythm centre (primarily responsible for regulating breathing).
Cardiovascular centre regulates heart rate and blood pressure.
Reflexes: swallowing, vomiting, coughing, sneezing; gastric secretion.
neetPoints: A chemosensitive area adjacent to the rhythm centre is highly sensitive to CO₂ and H⁺ ions.
The role of oxygen in regulating respiratory rhythm is quite insignificant.

mcqs.stem: The respiratory rhythm centre is located in the:
mcqs.explanation: It is in the medulla region of the brain.

mcqs.stem: The chemosensitive area near the respiratory rhythm centre is mainly sensitive to:
mcqs.explanation: Increase in CO₂ and H⁺ activates it to adjust breathing.

title: Cerebellum
junior: The cerebellum is the 'little brain' at the back of your head. It keeps you balanced and makes your movements smooth — like when you ride a bike or catch a ball.
definition: The cerebellum is part of the hindbrain with a very convoluted surface that provides additional space for many more neurons.
structure: Two hemispheres joined by the vermis.
Outer grey cortex with folia; inner white matter (arbor vitae).
functions: Coordinates voluntary movements, posture and balance.
Motor learning.
neetPoints: Its folded surface gives space for many more neurons.

mcqs.stem: The cerebellum has a very convoluted surface in order to:
options: Provide space for many more neurons
mcqs.explanation: NCERT: the convoluted surface provides additional space for many more neurons.

mcqs.stem: Damage to the cerebellum most likely causes:
mcqs.explanation: The cerebellum coordinates movement and balance.

title: Spinal cord
junior: The spinal cord is a thick bundle of nerves running down inside your backbone. It carries messages between your brain and body, and it can even react before your brain knows — like pulling your hand from something hot.
definition: The spinal cord is the part of the CNS that extends from the medulla through the neural canal of the vertebral column; it carries impulses to and from the brain and is the centre for spinal reflexes.
structure: Inner butterfly-shaped grey matter and outer white matter (opposite of the cerebrum).
31 pairs of spinal nerves; dorsal root (afferent, with dorsal root ganglion) and ventral root (efferent).
Central canal filled with cerebrospinal fluid.
functions: Conduction of impulses between the brain and the body.
Reflex actions: afferent neuron → dorsal root → spinal cord → efferent neuron → effector.
neetPoints: A reflex arc needs at least one afferent (sensory) and one efferent (motor) neuron.
The afferent neuron enters through the dorsal nerve root; the efferent neuron leaves through the ventral root.
Knee-jerk reflex is a classic example.
commonMistakes: Sensory (afferent) fibres enter the dorsal root; motor (efferent) fibres leave via the ventral root.

mcqs.stem: In a reflex arc, the afferent neuron enters the spinal cord through the:
mcqs.explanation: The afferent neuron receives the signal from a sensory organ and transmits it via the dorsal nerve root into the CNS.

mcqs.stem: In the spinal cord, grey matter is:
mcqs.explanation: The spinal cord has central grey matter and peripheral white matter.

title: Optic nerve
junior: The optic nerve is a thick cable from the back of each eye to your brain. It carries the pictures your eyes see.
definition: The optic nerve (cranial nerve II) carries visual impulses from the retina to the brain.
structure: Formed by axons of retinal ganglion cells.
Leaves the eye at the blind spot, where there are no photoreceptors.
The two nerves meet at the optic chiasma.
functions: Transmits visual information to the visual cortex (occipital lobe).
neetPoints: The blind spot is where the optic nerve leaves the eye and retinal blood vessels enter; it has no photoreceptor cells.

mcqs.stem: The optic nerve is formed by the axons of:
mcqs.explanation: Ganglion cell axons converge at the blind spot to form the optic nerve.

mcqs.stem: Why is there no image formation at the blind spot?
options: It is covered by the iris
mcqs.explanation: Photoreceptor cells are absent where the optic nerve leaves the eye.
